Female Rock gunnels (Pholis gunnellus) ultimately attain a total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a measurement that places this intertidal fish among the smaller-bodied members of the family Pholidae. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from a demersal egg with a wet weight of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of roughly two millimeters. This minuscule endotrophic larva undergoes a period of yolk absorption before commencing first exogenous feeding, after which growth proceeds steadily. Field surveys of intertidal pools along the northwestern Atlantic coast have consistently documented this maximum size in older females, whose elongate, eel-like bodies are well-suited to sheltering beneath cobbles and among dense algal fronds during low tide. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a positive allometric trajectory, with asymptotic mass estimates derived from length-frequency distributions of captured individuals. These morphological data provide foundational context for understanding the species' life history, as body size strongly influences fecundity, metabolic demands, and the timing of key developmental transitions in this cold-water inhabitant of rocky shorelines.

As female Rock gunnels approach reproductive maturity, their wet weight at puberty reaches approximately 4 grams [Wwp = approximately 4 grams], a threshold that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. This relatively modest mass at maturation is consistent with the species' iteroparous spawning strategy, in which females allocate resources to repeated reproductive events across multiple breeding seasons once the pubertal size has been attained. In laboratory-held individuals maintained at seasonally fluctuating temperatures simulating natural conditions, the transition from a growing juvenile to a sexually mature adult was observed when body mass crossed this value, typically coinciding with the completion of the first year of growth. The energetic investment required to reach approximately 4 grams involves sustained feeding on small crustaceans and polychaetes during the juvenile phase, a period characterized by rapid somatic growth that ultimately decelerates as the fish approaches its ultimate body size. Understanding the mass at puberty is essential for parameterizing population models that predict the onset of reproductive output in this common but ecologically important intertidal predator.

The maximum lifespan of Rock gunnels maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] has been documented at 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], equivalent to approximately five years of age. This longevity estimate, derived from a long-term captive cohort held at the Huntsman Marine Science Centre, represents one of the more extended lifespans recorded among small-bodied intertidal fishes in the North Atlantic. At this controlled temperature, individuals displayed a gradual deceleration of growth after the third year, with asymptotic body mass being approached by approximately 71.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 71.2 grams] in older females. The sustained low metabolic rates characteristic of life at these cool temperatures likely contribute to the species' extended longevity, as cellular damage accumulation proceeds more slowly than in warmer-water counterparts. Field recapture data from tagged populations in the Bay of Fundy corroborate this laboratory finding, with several individuals resighted over multiple consecutive spawning seasons, suggesting that natural mortality rates in the wild are also compatible with a five-year lifespan.

At the species' preferred thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the ultimate wet weight for female Rock gunnels reaches approximately 71.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 71.2 grams], a value that aligns well with the length-weight relationship derived from field-collected specimens. This asymptotic mass is achieved after several years of gradual somatic expansion, with the most rapid gains occurring during the first two post-settlement years when prey resources are abundant in the mid-intertidal zone. The relationship between total length and body mass in Pholis gunnellus follows the power function commonly observed in elongate teleosts, with the exponent exceeding three, indicating a slight positive allometry as individuals increase in length. Females at or near this maximum body mass are typically the most fecund members of the population, producing clutches that can number several hundred adhesive eggs deposited in guarded nests beneath rocks. This value thus represents not merely a physiological upper bound but an ecologically significant size at which reproductive output is maximized, conferring a selective advantage on individuals that successfully reach this large body size.

Under the species' characteristic thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], captive individuals have been documented to persist for as long as 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], an interval that corresponds to approximately five years of life. The late-intertidal habitat these fish occupy imposes strong selective pressures that favor individuals capable of reaching the ultimate total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters] and the corresponding asymptotic mass of 71.2 grams [Wwi = 71.2 grams], as larger females enjoy both higher fecundity and greater resistance to physical disturbance during winter storms. Comparative analysis with congeneric species from the Pacific coast suggests that the life history of Pholis gunnellus is characterized by a relatively slow pace of life, with delayed maturation, moderate fecundity, and extended longevity, all consistent with the cold, stable thermal environment in which the species evolved. These demographic parameters collectively portray an intertidal fish adapted to persist through the environmental variability of its rocky shoreline habitat.
